title: The City of Mithila
captions: From Gautama's hermitage, the sages and the princes walked on to Mithila. King Janaka's great yajna was taking place there, and rishis had come from many lands. “What a wonderful gathering!” said Rama.
When King Janaka heard that Sage Vishvamitra had arrived, he hurried out at once. His priest Shatananda walked in front, and other priests followed, carrying water and offerings to welcome the guest.
Janaka bowed low and offered the sage water, a seat and his respect. “By your coming, great sage, my yajna is truly blessed,” he said with joy.

Then Janaka looked at the two princes. “Who are these young heroes, who walk like lions and shine like devas?” he asked. Vishvamitra told him they were the sons of King Dasharatha, and had come to see the great bow.

Vishvamitra also told how Rama had set Ahalya free. Shatananda, the eldest son of Gautama and Ahalya, was filled with joy. “Is my mother truly free? Is she with my father again?” he asked. “Yes,” said the sage.
Shatananda folded his hands and thanked Rama with all his heart. Then he told the princes the wonderful story of how Vishvamitra, once a mighty king, became a great rishi through long years of tapas.
As the sun began to set, King Janaka bowed to Vishvamitra. “Please rest well, honoured guests,” he said. “I will see you again in the morning.” Then he returned to his palace.
story: From Gautama's hermitage, the travellers walked on to Mithila. King Janaka's great yajna was taking place there, and rishis had come from many lands. Rama was amazed by the wonderful gathering.

When King Janaka heard that Vishvamitra had arrived, he hurried out at once. His priest Shatananda walked in front, and other priests followed with water and offerings. Janaka bowed low and offered the sage water, a seat and his respect.

Then Janaka noticed the two princes. He asked who these young heroes were, who walked like lions and shone like devas. Vishvamitra told him they were the sons of King Dasharatha, and that they had come to see the great bow.

Vishvamitra also told how Rama had set Ahalya free. Shatananda was the eldest son of Gautama and Ahalya, and his heart filled with joy to hear that his mother was free and with his father again. He thanked Rama with folded hands.

Then Shatananda told the princes how Vishvamitra, once a mighty king, had become a great rishi through long years of tapas. As the sun set, Janaka bowed to his guests, wished them a good rest and promised to see them in the morning.
lesson: When Vishvamitra and the princes arrived, King Janaka did not wait for them to come to his palace. He hurried out himself, offered them water and a seat, listened to their story and made sure they could rest in comfort. In our tradition we say “Atithi Devo Bhava”, which means the guest is like God. Our elders teach that Atithi seva, caring for a guest with a warm heart, is a joy and a blessing for the whole home.
lesson_long: Atithi seva means caring for a guest with a warm heart.

King Janaka was a great king, busy with an important yajna. Still, he did not wait for his guests to come to him. He hurried out himself, offered water and a seat, listened to their story and made sure they could rest in comfort.
Our elders teach that welcoming a guest is a joy and a blessing for the whole home. A glass of water and a kind word can make someone feel truly at home.
tradition: The Taittiriya Upanishad gives students four short teachings: Matru Devo Bhava, Pitru Devo Bhava, Acharya Devo Bhava, Atithi Devo Bhava. They mean: treat your mother, your father, your teacher and your guest as God.
That is why, in many Hindu homes, a guest is first offered water, then a seat, then food. These simple steps come from the old way of welcoming, and families still follow them today.
words: a great sage who sees deep truths
question: When a guest comes to our home, what can you do to make them feel welcome?
questions: When a guest comes to our home, what can you do to make them feel welcome?

card_lesson: King Janaka hurried out to welcome his guests with water, a seat and great respect. Our elders teach “Atithi Devo Bhava”: a guest is like God, and should feel truly at home.
